sources.entry: AMD's Turin: 5th Gen EPYC Launched - Measures what wider die-to-IO links and faster DDR5 do for Turin bandwidth, and where latency rose over Genoa.

summary.title: AMD's Turin: 5th Gen EPYC Launched
summary.one_liner: Hands-on look at AMD's EPYC 9575F (Turin) showing how wider die-to-IO links and DDR5 speeds change memory bandwidth, and where latency rose compared with Genoa.
takeaways: The 9575F reaches about 52 GB/s single-thread read bandwidth, and nearly 99% of the 576 GB/s theoretical full-socket read bandwidth.
Turin's server CCDs use GMI3-W with two GMI links to the IO die (vs one on desktop Zen 5), and a 32B-per-link write path, which raises per-CCD bandwidth.
Memory speed depends on configuration: DDR5-6400 only on validated 1DPC systems, DDR5-6000 typical, 4400 MT/s at 2DPC.
Unloaded memory latency is similar to Genoa, but core-to-core latency rose, especially within a CCD (~45 ns intra-CCD, ~150 ns inter-CCD, ~260 ns socket-to-socket).
summary.summary: Chips and Cheese tests AMD's EPYC 9575F, a Turin server CPU, focusing on memory subsystem changes rather than the Zen 5 core, which they had already covered. They measure single-thread and full-socket bandwidth for read, write and add operations, socket-to-socket bandwidth, and unloaded and loaded latency, using a loaded-latency test where 7 cores or CCDs run bandwidth load while the 8th measures latency. They also report clock speeds under single-thread, Cinebench 2024 and web-server workloads. The conclusion frames Turin as an evolutionary update similar to Milan to Genoa rather than a major step change.
